prompt.context_jp: 画面の中では深沢がMERを誇らしげに見ている。
prompt.prompt_jp: しかし、その現場に立ち会ったばかりの比奈の顔___、素直に喜べぬまま曇っていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that best fits the contrast with Fukazawa's reaction.

feedback.correct_en: は marks a contrastive topic: unlike Fukazawa who is proud, Hina's face by contrast was clouded. The 「しかし」 signals the contrast explicitly.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would introduce Hina's face as new information, missing the explicit contrast with the previous sentence about Fukazawa.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は喜んだが、彼女の顔は曇った。
contrast_examples.en: He was happy, but her face (by contrast) was clouded.

contrast_examples.jp: ドアが開いて、彼女が入ってきた。
contrast_examples.en: The door opened and she (new info) came in.

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見先生の評価について聞かれた比奈の答え。
prompt.prompt_jp: うーん 腕___ いいと思う
prompt.prompt_en: Pick the particle that fits this evaluation of Kitami's skill.

feedback.correct_en: は narrows the topic to just 'his skill' with an implicit contrast — his skill is good (but other things, like his methods, aren't). This matches Hina's next lines criticizing his approach.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would just assert 'his skill is good' as new info with no reservation, losing the 'but...' nuance that Hina clearly carries.

contrast_examples.jp: 味はいいけど、値段は高い。
contrast_examples.en: The taste is good (but price is high).

contrast_examples.jp: あっ、味がいい！
contrast_examples.en: Oh, the taste is good! (fresh discovery)

prompt.context_jp: 比奈が喜多見チーフを批判する場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: だけど 喜多見チーフがやってること___ 医者のやることじゃない
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that frames 'what Chief Kitami is doing' as the topic being judged.

feedback.correct_en: は sets up 'what Kitami does' as the topic, about which a judgment ('isn't a doctor's job') follows. This is classic topic–comment structure for an evaluation.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present it as new information being identified, but here Hina is commenting ON a known subject, not identifying who does what.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の方法は危険だ。
contrast_examples.en: His method is dangerous. (comment on topic)

contrast_examples.jp: 誰がやったの？彼がやった。
contrast_examples.en: Who did it? He did. (identification)

prompt.context_jp: 高輪が部長会での議論を説明している。
prompt.prompt_jp: 出動要請___ あると 病院の看護師や研修医が 駆り出される
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for 'dispatch request' in this conditional clause.

feedback.correct_en: Inside a subordinate 〜と clause describing a triggering event, が marks the event-introducing subject ('when a request comes in'). は would wrongly promote it to the main-clause topic.
feedback.incorrect_en: は inside this kind of conditional/temporal clause sounds unnatural — it would try to make 'dispatch request' the overall topic rather than the triggering event.

contrast_examples.jp: 電話が鳴ると、彼女は出た。
contrast_examples.en: When the phone rang, she answered.

contrast_examples.jp: 電話は鳴らなかった。
contrast_examples.en: The phone didn't ring. (topic/contrast)

prompt.context_jp: 音羽が各機関の反応を報告している。
prompt.prompt_jp: 特に 爆発の危険___ あったバス内に 安全確認をせずに 侵入したことは…
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle marking 'danger of explosion' inside this relative clause.

feedback.correct_en: Inside a relative clause modifying バス ('a bus that had danger of explosion'), が marks the subject of 'had'. Subordinate clauses typically take が, not は.
feedback.incorrect_en: は inside a relative clause breaks the structure — it would try to make 'danger' the sentence-level topic, which doesn't fit.

contrast_examples.jp: 人が多い店
contrast_examples.en: a shop where there are many people

contrast_examples.jp: この店は人が多い。
contrast_examples.en: This shop has many people. (main-clause topic)

prompt.context_jp: 関係機関の反応は悪いと聞いた直後、冬木が尋ねる。
prompt.prompt_jp: ですけど 世間の反応___いいんですよね
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle fitting the contrast with officialdom's bad reaction.

feedback.correct_en: は carries a contrastive sense here: officialdom hates MER, but 'the public's reaction' (as opposed to theirs) is good, right? The ですけど signals this contrast.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would just assert the public reaction as a new fact without contrasting it against the earlier bad news, missing the point of the question.

contrast_examples.jp: 上司は反対だけど、同僚は賛成だ。
contrast_examples.en: The boss opposes it, but colleagues (by contrast) agree.

contrast_examples.jp: 反応がいい！
contrast_examples.en: The reaction is good! (fresh observation)

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見が医師の役割を語る。
prompt.prompt_jp: 医者にできるの___ ただ 目の前の命を救うことだけですよ
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for 'what a doctor can do'.

feedback.correct_en: は marks 'what a doctor can do' as the topic, with the comment identifying its single content (saving lives). The nominalized のは…だけ frame is a classic topic-definition pattern.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would turn this into an identificational 'it is X that a doctor can do', which doesn't match the のは…だけです frame Kitami uses to define his philosophy.

contrast_examples.jp: 大事なのは命だ。
contrast_examples.en: What's important is life. (topic-comment)

contrast_examples.jp: 命が大事だ。
contrast_examples.en: Life is important. (plain assertion)

prompt.context_jp: 比奈がMERの構成を説明する。
prompt.prompt_jp: ＭＥＲの専属スタッフ___ チーフドクターの 喜多見先生だけです
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that singles out Kitami as the sole exclusive member.

feedback.correct_en: は presents 'MER's exclusive staff' as the topic, and the comment specifies it is only Kitami. The 'X is Y だけです' pattern typically takes は on X.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would push toward an exhaustive-listing reading ('it's Kitami who is...'), but the sentence structure here is a topic-definition, not identification of 'who among candidates'.

contrast_examples.jp: 専属は彼だけです。
contrast_examples.en: The exclusive one is only him. (topic)

contrast_examples.jp: 誰が専属？——彼が専属です。
contrast_examples.en: Who's exclusive? — He is. (identification)

prompt.context_jp: 比奈の心に浮かぶイメージ。
prompt.prompt_jp: 高輪の顔___、ふと胸の内に浮かんでくる。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for 'Takanawa's face' as it springs to mind.

feedback.correct_en: が marks the subject of a spontaneous event ('a face suddenly comes to mind') — new, unplanned information surfacing. ふと also typically pairs with が in such sudden-emergence contexts.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make 'Takanawa's face' a pre-established topic, contradicting the 'suddenly comes to mind' spontaneity.

contrast_examples.jp: ふと母の顔が浮かんだ。
contrast_examples.en: My mother's face suddenly came to mind.

contrast_examples.jp: 母の顔はよく思い出す。
contrast_examples.en: I often recall my mother's face. (habitual topic)

prompt.context_jp: 赤塚が国と東京の対立を説明する。
prompt.prompt_jp: 国___私が立ち上げたＭＥＲに 失敗の烙印を押して 潰したがっている
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for 'the national government' in this contrast with Tokyo.

feedback.correct_en: は marks 国 as the contrastive topic — 'as for the national government (as opposed to Tokyo), they want to crush MER'. The preceding sentence sets up the Tokyo vs. nation contrast.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would present 国 as new information identifying who wants to crush MER, but Akatsuka is making a thematic statement, not answering 'who'.

contrast_examples.jp: 東京は味方、国は敵だ。
contrast_examples.en: Tokyo is an ally; the nation (by contrast) is the enemy.

contrast_examples.jp: どこが潰したい？——国が潰したい。
contrast_examples.en: Who wants to crush it? — The nation does. (identification)

prompt.context_jp: 白金が音羽の報告を伝える。
prompt.prompt_jp: 派遣した医系技官の報告では チーフの喜多見というの___ ずいぶん ムチャを やっているようでして
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for 'the one called Chief Kitami'.

feedback.correct_en: Here が marks 喜多見というの as the subject of a report clause — the content of the report. In embedded 'ようです' content, が naturally marks the acting subject.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would thematize Kitami as the broader topic, but the sentence is reporting what Kitami is doing as the content observed, so が fits better.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が暴走しているようだ。
contrast_examples.en: It seems he's going wild.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は暴走している。
contrast_examples.en: He is (as for him) going wild. (topic)

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見のスピーチ。
prompt.prompt_jp: 東京全体の救命救急___ カバーすることは できません
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle marking the object of カバーする.

feedback.correct_en: カバーする takes a direct object marked by を — 'to cover all of Tokyo's emergency care'.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would be ungrammatical here with the transitive カバーする following; に would mean 'to/into', which doesn't fit 'cover X'.

contrast_examples.jp: 地域をカバーする。
contrast_examples.en: to cover the region

contrast_examples.jp: 保険が適用される。
contrast_examples.en: insurance applies (intransitive, が)

prompt.context_jp: 音羽が喜多見の理想論を批判する。
prompt.prompt_jp: だけど 現実___甘くない
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle contrasting 'reality' with 'ideals'.

feedback.correct_en: は contrasts 現実 with the preceding '理想' — ideals feel nice, BUT reality (by contrast) isn't sweet. The だけど cue reinforces this contrastive-topic use.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would just assert reality's harshness as new info, missing the explicit理想/現実 contrast the speaker is drawing.

contrast_examples.jp: 理想は美しいが、現実は厳しい。
contrast_examples.en: Ideals are beautiful, but reality (by contrast) is harsh.

contrast_examples.jp: 現実が見えてきた。
contrast_examples.en: Reality has come into view. (new info)

prompt.context_jp: 音羽が比奈に証言を迫る。
prompt.prompt_jp: 内部にいる弦巻先生___ 喜多見チーフを批判すれば 組織解体に向け 一気に流れが傾くはずです
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for 'Dr. Tsurumaki, who is on the inside' in this conditional.

feedback.correct_en: Inside a 〜ば conditional clause, が marks the subject of the hypothetical action ('if YOU, an insider, criticize him...'). The subject is also being singled out as the key actor.
feedback.incorrect_en: は inside this subordinate conditional clause would wrongly try to make 弦巻先生 the main topic of the whole sentence.

contrast_examples.jp: あなたが言えば、みんな信じる。
contrast_examples.en: If you say it, everyone will believe.

contrast_examples.jp: あなたは信頼されている。
contrast_examples.en: You are trusted. (main-clause topic)

prompt.context_jp: ミーティング前の比奈。
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼女はもう一度肩の力___抜こうと深く息を吐いた。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle for 'tension in the shoulders'.

feedback.correct_en: 力を抜く is a set collocation meaning 'relax/let out the tension'. The direct object 力 takes を.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make 力 the subject, which is wrong since 抜く is transitive here; に has no meaning fit.

contrast_examples.jp: 肩の力を抜いて。
contrast_examples.en: Relax your shoulders.

contrast_examples.jp: 力が抜けた。
contrast_examples.en: My strength drained away. (intransitive, 抜ける)

prompt.context_jp: 深沢の軽口。
prompt.prompt_jp: どこの___かも分からない医者に 新しい組織 任せていいのかって
prompt.prompt_en: Fill in the idiomatic phrase meaning 'nobody of known origin'.

feedback.correct_en: 「どこの馬の骨か分からない」 is a fixed idiom meaning 'someone of unknown background/pedigree' — dismissive. It fits the gossip tone exactly.
feedback.incorrect_en: 犬の骨 and 猫の毛 are not idioms; only 馬の骨 is the conventional set phrase.

contrast_examples.jp: どこの馬の骨か分からない男と結婚するな。
contrast_examples.en: Don't marry a man of unknown background.

contrast_examples.jp: 素性のはっきりしない人物。
contrast_examples.en: a person of unclear origin (neutral)

prompt.context_jp: 比奈の喜多見評を聞いた同僚の反応。
prompt.prompt_jp: ___褒めじゃん
prompt.prompt_en: Fill in the intensifier meaning 'nothing but praise'.

feedback.correct_en: 「べた褒め」 means 'lavish/all-out praise'. It is a common colloquial compound.
feedback.incorrect_en: ばり褒め and ぺた褒め are not standard words. べた is the correct prefix for 'uniformly/thoroughly'.

contrast_examples.jp: 上司にべた褒めされた。
contrast_examples.en: My boss praised me to the skies.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼を絶賛した。
contrast_examples.en: They praised him highly. (more formal)

prompt.context_jp: 高輪が受け入れの経緯を話す。
prompt.prompt_jp: 赤塚知事から ___に 要請 受けちゃったんだから
prompt.prompt_en: Fill in the adverb meaning 'personally/directly from the person himself'.

feedback.correct_en: 「じきじきに」 means 'personally, directly from the person himself' — fitting a direct request from the governor.
feedback.incorrect_en: ぎりぎり means 'barely/at the last moment'; そろそろ means 'about time'. Neither fits a personal request.

contrast_examples.jp: 社長からじきじきにお願いされた。
contrast_examples.en: The president personally asked me.

contrast_examples.jp: ぎりぎりで間に合った。
contrast_examples.en: I barely made it in time.

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見がMER批判を気にしない様子で。
prompt.prompt_jp: こんなもんでしょ 新しい組織に対する ___なんて
prompt.prompt_en: Fill in the noun meaning 'headwind / hostile pressure against'.

feedback.correct_en: 「風当たり」 literally 'wind-hitting', idiomatically means 'criticism/hostile pressure' aimed at someone or something new.
feedback.incorrect_en: 風通し means 'ventilation/openness'; 風向き means 'wind direction / trend'. Only 風当たり captures 'social backlash'.

contrast_examples.jp: 新人への風当たりが強い。
contrast_examples.en: Pressure on newcomers is strong.

contrast_examples.jp: 風向きが変わった。
contrast_examples.en: The tide has turned.

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見が比奈を誘う。
prompt.prompt_jp: 一緒に汗 ___ますか？
prompt.prompt_en: Fill in the verb that collocates with 汗 to mean 'break a sweat'.

feedback.correct_en: 「汗を流す」 is the standard collocation for 'sweat / work up a sweat (together)'. It also idiomatically suggests exercising together.
feedback.incorrect_en: 汗を落とす could mean 'wash off sweat' (shower), not exercise; 汗を切る isn't a natural collocation.

contrast_examples.jp: 一緒に汗を流しましょう。
contrast_examples.en: Let's work up a sweat together.

contrast_examples.jp: シャワーで汗を落とす。
contrast_examples.en: wash off sweat in the shower

prompt.context_jp: 赤塚が音羽について警告する。
prompt.prompt_jp: あの人は間違いなく 白金の___がかかった敵よ
prompt.prompt_en: Fill in the noun forming the idiom 'under X's influence / X's agent'.

feedback.correct_en: 「息がかかる」 is an idiom meaning 'to be under someone's influence/patronage' — exactly fitting 'Shirokane's agent'.
feedback.incorrect_en: 手がかかる means 'to require effort/trouble'; 目がかかる is not a standard idiom in this sense.

contrast_examples.jp: 大臣の息がかかった人物。
contrast_examples.en: a person under the minister's influence

contrast_examples.jp: この子は手がかかる。
contrast_examples.en: This child is a handful.

prompt.context_jp: 白金が赤塚の笑顔を評する。
prompt.prompt_jp: 梓スマイル 笑ってる時は 大抵 ___なのよね
prompt.prompt_en: Fill in the idiom meaning 'two-faced / saying one thing and meaning another'.

feedback.correct_en: 「二枚舌」 literally 'two tongues' means 'speaking with a forked tongue / two-faced'. It fits Shirokane's cynical take on Akatsuka.
feedback.incorrect_en: 三枚舌 is not standard. 二枚目 means 'a handsome man / leading-man role' — completely different.

contrast_examples.jp: あの政治家は二枚舌だ。
contrast_examples.en: That politician is two-faced.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は二枚目俳優だ。
contrast_examples.en: He's a handsome lead actor.

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見のバツイチが発覚した場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 人は___によらぬもの
prompt.prompt_en: Fill in the noun completing the proverb 'you can't judge X by appearance'.

feedback.correct_en: 「人は見かけによらぬもの」 is a set proverb — 'you can't judge a person by appearances'. The fixed form uses 見かけ.
feedback.incorrect_en: 外見 has similar meaning but is not the fixed form of this proverb; 中身 ('contents') reverses the sense entirely.

contrast_examples.jp: 人は見かけによらぬものだ。
contrast_examples.en: You can't judge people by appearance.

contrast_examples.jp: 外見より中身が大事。
contrast_examples.en: What's inside matters more than looks.

prompt.context_jp: 兼務への不満を話す比奈。原文の響きに近いのはどちら？
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds most natural as Hina's casual complaint to a friend?

choices.text: 当たり前でしょ 循環器外科と兼務なんて ありえないって
当然です。循環器外科との兼務は不可能だと申し上げたい。

feedback.correct_en: Option A matches the casual, exasperated register appropriate for complaining to a close colleague — でしょ, なんて, って ending.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B uses formal, stiff business language (申し上げたい) that would be jarring in a break-room gripe between friends.

contrast_examples.jp: ありえないって！
contrast_examples.en: No way, seriously! (casual venting)

contrast_examples.jp: ありえないと存じます。
contrast_examples.en: I believe it is impossible. (overly formal)

prompt.context_jp: 音羽が立場を明らかにする場面。公式な自己定義として自然なのは？
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing sounds most natural for Otowa's formal self-positioning?

choices.text: 私は 医師である前に 厚労省から派遣された官僚です
俺はさ、医者っていうより官僚なんだよね

feedback.correct_en: Option A — the actual line — uses です and the formal 'である前に' pattern, matching Otowa's bureaucratic register.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B uses rough first-person 俺 and sentence-ending よね in a chatty way — inappropriate for Otowa clarifying his official role to the team.

contrast_examples.jp: 医師である前に官僚です。
contrast_examples.en: Before being a doctor, I am a bureaucrat. (formal)

contrast_examples.jp: 医者っていうより官僚だよ。
contrast_examples.en: More of a bureaucrat than a doctor, really. (casual)

prompt.context_jp: 音羽に助力を頼む冬木。やんわりお願いするのに自然なのは？
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing most naturally softens the request for help?

choices.text: ここは ひとつ 音羽先生の お力で 何とかなりませんか？
音羽先生の力でなんとかしろよ

feedback.correct_en: Option A — the real line — uses the softener 「ここはひとつ」 and the polite indirect 「何とかなりませんか」, appropriate for pleading with a superior-like figure.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B uses the imperative しろよ, which is blunt and demanding — not how a team member would address Otowa in this scene.

contrast_examples.jp: ここはひとつ、お願いできませんか。
contrast_examples.en: Could I ask you for just this once? (softened)

contrast_examples.jp: なんとかしろ。
contrast_examples.en: Fix it! (blunt command)

prompt.context_jp: 赤塚が記者会見で政治意図を否定する発言。もっとも自然なのは？
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing fits a governor's public press-conference denial most naturally?

choices.text: 政治的な意図は一切ございません
政治的な意図はまったくないよ

feedback.correct_en: Option A — the real line — uses ございません, the humble-polite denial expected in formal press statements by a public official.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B's casual ないよ would be totally out of place in a televised press conference by a governor.

contrast_examples.jp: そのような意図は一切ございません。
contrast_examples.en: We harbor no such intent whatsoever. (press-conference formal)

contrast_examples.jp: そんなつもりないよ。
contrast_examples.en: I don't mean that. (casual chat)

prompt.context_jp: 音羽が、プライベートな付き合いを断る場面として自然なのは？
prompt.prompt_en: Which line sounds most natural for Otowa's cool refusal of after-hours socializing?

choices.text: プライベートまで踏み込む つきあいは嫌いなんです
プライベートまで踏み込むつきあいはやだな～

feedback.correct_en: Option A — the real line — uses the controlled 嫌いなんです, matching Otowa's cool, formal distance.
feedback.incorrect_en: Option B's やだな～ is childish/casual and clashes with Otowa's bureaucratic, standoffish persona.

contrast_examples.jp: そういうのは嫌いなんです。
contrast_examples.en: I'm not fond of that sort of thing. (cool, polite)

contrast_examples.jp: そういうのやだな～。
contrast_examples.en: Ewww, I don't like that. (childish casual)
